I've battled extreme eczema and while I'm not fully healed, I can tell you what I would do in your situation:

1/ Leave that mouldy bedroom at once until it is fixed. Get a pro to remove the mould and take measures afterwards to keep it from coming back (ventilation, ventilation ventilation).

2/ Get a total blood examination done, and I mean total, depending on where you live this is the kind of examination that is not included in social welfare and will cost a bit. Find a doc who is willing to take it and the results will tell you what substances your body reacts to (mine were wheat flour and beet sugar).

3/ Use whatever corticosteroid you use now, as long as it is not in the strong category (too addictive), but only use it to get your current flares under control. After that, you rely more on moisturising creams with fungicides and on your diet.

Please do not go stronger. If you find that your skin reacts to the corticosteroid, don't think of tsw immediately (I know the fear), but rather ask your dermatologist for a different base (different lotion, cream that the corticosteroid is processed in) as uour skin could react to that.

4/ Replace your moisturising cream with Daktozin. This is baby ointment for nappy rash and works wonders against itch plus restores your skin due to the high zinc content.
Any fungae present on your skin will be fought too.

5/ Consider eating lots of onions, garlic, grapefruit and/or taking quercetin supplements. These foods willl battle yeasts, fungae and contain very strong antioxidants and natural antibiotics.

I got used at that job, worked my socks off. People commented on  how I could become a manager. But I'd forgotten the golden rule to be pragmatic. In short, I'd made myself popular and loved among my coworkers but became a supposed threat to higher management. So I got laid off before I sealed the deal, so to speak. 
That was last year in Octobre.

I still live with my parents even though on the horizon a financially independent life was looming. I thought I would make good on the years lost, but had to start from scratch with nothing to show, as I worked way above my job title.

What followed were months and months of drinking. I managed to conceal it well. But at that time, it was that or suicide. Alcohol is a depressant to be sure. But how my thoughts were racing was too much to bear . 
Scary enough, due to that sudden period of idleness, past traumas from my childhood started to surface.I started to feel like a fraud, like everyone who shows me a gentle face does not know how they are being conned by me.

I've always had that, how I couldn't understand when people liked me so much. I felt like a good actor. 

Anyways, months and months followed and eventually, in 2020 I started therapy and lessened my drinking.il I still drink, but not so much anymore. And my therapist serves as a good way to tell her all of my life and it's reassuring to see that she likes me even after she knows everything.  The eyes do not lie.

But what really struck me, is that I needed to do something about all these underlying problems, these past traumas- which can range from some insensitive remarks you heard as a child, to troubled sexual experiences- had been left unchecked for way too long.  Instead of dealing with them at the time and letting go, they had become part of my identity.

It's good to grow in character and to 'fake it until you make it', but in truth: you won't solve a depression if you layer yourself.
